title: What a Small Side Project Teaches You
summary: Side projects show you the whole path from idea to release. What recovery research says about them, and how to keep one fun instead of turning it into a second job.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's 9 p.m. and you've opened a folder called tmp-budget for the third time this month. Every month you copy numbers from three banking apps into a spreadsheet by hand, and tonight you've decided a 40-line script should do it for you. No ticket, no stakeholder, no sprint. Just you, an annoying chore and an editor.

That's how most side projects start, and it's a great place to learn. This post is about why that small, slightly messy folder is worth something, and about the point where it stops helping and starts eating your rest.

A place where trying things is cheap

At work, every change is tied to something: a deadline, a reviewer, a legacy constraint, a customer who'll notice. That's how it should be. It also means trying a new idea has a price, and someone has to sign off on it. A side project skips the sign-off. You can try a new framework, write a tiny parser or build a clumsy first version just to see how it feels. The worst case is a lost evening.

The good ones usually start with a personal itch, like that budget script. You're the user, so you find out right away whether it works: either the chore got shorter this month or it didn't. You don't need a motivational poster. You need the problem to keep bugging you.

You get to walk the whole path

On a team, someone owns the backend, someone else the frontend, another person the deploy pipeline. In a side project, even a tiny one, you meet every step: scope, data model, UI, error states, deploy, docs, and the part nobody warns you about, maintenance. You learn why a simple feature gets complicated once it has users, even when the only user is you six weeks later, squinting at your own code.

Simon Willison, one of the creators of Django, keeps an absurd number of open-source side projects alive: 185 Python packages at the time of his 2022 DjangoCon talk. His trick is borrowing habits from big teams. Every project starts with a test, the docs live in the same repo as the code, and work starts as an issue so he can return to a project months later without relearning it (Coping strategies for the serial project hoarder). He also warns against side projects with user accounts, because those turn into unpaid jobs. That's a lot of real engineering practice picked up from something you build for fun.

Side projects also show you your own taste. What do you cut when you only have two evenings? Which names still make sense a month later? When does one more feature become clutter? Once you've made those calls yourself, your opinions at work get less secondhand. You've paid for the trade-off instead of reading about it.

One of mine is Glance, a macOS menu bar app that translates selected text between English and Vietnamese. It has no backend of its own: the text goes only to the translation engine (Google Translate by default), and the download is under 1 MB. Even a tool that small needed more than the translating part: packaging, cutting a release and a README that tells people exactly where their text goes. A ticket rarely shows you that whole picture.

Rest, or a second job?

To be honest, not everyone should code in the evenings, and nobody should feel guilty for skipping it. People already spend their energy on work, family, health and a life away from screens.

Research on recovery helps draw the line. Sabine Sonnentag and Charlotte Fritz describe four ways people recover from work in their free time: mentally detaching from work, relaxing, "mastery" (taking on a challenge and learning something new) and control over how you spend that time (The Recovery Experience Questionnaire, 2007). A healthy side project sits in mastery and control. You picked it, you set the pace, you learn something. A "side project" that's really work tickets you took home because you felt you should gives you neither, and it eats your detachment too.

There's also some evidence that the good kind pays off at work. Kevin Eschleman and colleagues studied 341 employees, then 92 U.S. Air Force captains whose coworkers and subordinates rated their performance. Creative activity outside work was linked with better recovery, and with more creative problem solving and more helping others on the job (ScienceDaily's summary of the 2014 study). It's a correlation, so it doesn't prove a hobby makes you better at your job. It does suggest that building things for fun and doing good work get along fine.

A quick check

If you skipped your side project this week, would you feel relieved or a little sad? Relief means it has turned into a chore. Pause it. A good side project gives you energy more often than it takes it.

Unfinished still counts

Most side-project folders never become products, and that's fine. They become cheap lessons: the idea was too broad, the stack didn't fit, the chore wasn't painful enough to automate. On a work project, learning that late can cost a team months. In a side project it costs a few evenings.

Keep it small enough to survive real life. One page that works beats a platform that never launches. A script that saves ten minutes every Friday beats a grand tool you now have to babysit. When the project starts making you feel guilty, pause it, cut it down, or let it end and keep what it taught you.

Over time the lessons add up. A toy login demo helps the day a real auth bug lands on your desk. A half-finished notes app teaches you data modeling. A small AI agent you built for yourself shows you where automation helps and where a person still has to check the result. None of them looks important on its own. Together they're a library of experience nobody assigned you. If you like the idea of one small learning goal at a time, One New Language a Year applies the same thinking to programming languages.

Try this week

  • Write down one chore that annoyed you at least twice this month. That's your project.
  • Size it to something you could finish in two or three evenings.
  • Start with one test and a short README, so future you can pick it back up.
  • Skip user accounts and anything other people depend on, unless you want a second job.
  • If it stops being fun, pause it. No guilt required.

faqs.q: Do I need side projects to get hired as a developer?
faqs.a: No. A side project can show an interviewer how you think when nobody handed you a spec, which helps most when you're early in your career or switching fields. Plenty of strong engineers have none. Work you can explain in detail, from your job or a course, counts just as much.

faqs.q: How do I stop a side project from turning into a second job?
faqs.a: Keep it small, avoid features other people depend on (Simon Willison specifically warns against user accounts) and pay attention to how it feels. Sabine Sonnentag and Charlotte Fritz count learning something new and controlling your own free time among the ways people recover from work. If the project feels like an obligation, it has stopped doing that, so pause it.

faqs.q: Is an unfinished side project a waste of time?
faqs.a: Usually not. It tells you cheaply that an idea was too broad, a stack didn't fit or a problem wasn't worth automating. Spending a few evenings to learn that beats finding out months into a work project.
